# Convection

Lecture 18 · [Original notes](https://www.alucasphys.com/p7810s2026/p7810s2026_lecture18.pdf)

::: {.callout-tip title="Learning objectives"}
Derive a temperature equation from energy and entropy conservation, identify Brinkman and Prandtl numbers, estimate thermal boundary layers, formulate the Boussinesq approximation, and compare viscous and inertial natural convection estimates.
:::

## Separating kinetic and internal energy {#sec-l18-energy}

Thermal transport requires restoring the energy equation. Let $e$ be internal energy per unit mass, $s$ entropy per unit mass, and $\tau_{ij}$ the viscous stress. Total energy density is

$$
\mathcal U=\frac12\rho v^2+\rho e.
$$

Mass and momentum conservation are

$$
D_t\rho=-\rho\nabla\cdot\mathbf v,
\qquad
\rho D_tv_i=-\partial_iP+\partial_j\tau_{ij}.
$$

For a Newtonian three dimensional fluid,

$$
\tau_{ij}=\eta\left(\partial_iv_j+\partial_jv_i-
\frac23\delta_{ij}\nabla\cdot\mathbf v\right)
+\zeta\delta_{ij}\nabla\cdot\mathbf v,
$$

where $\zeta$ is bulk viscosity. Fourier's heat flux is $\mathbf q=-\kappa\nabla T$. Subtracting the kinetic energy equation from total energy conservation yields

$$
\rho D_te=-P\nabla\cdot\mathbf v
+\tau_{ij}\partial_jv_i+\nabla\cdot(\kappa\nabla T).
$$ {#eq-l18-internal}

The first term is compression work, the second viscous conversion of mechanical energy into heat, and the last conduction.

## Supplemental derivation: entropy to temperature {#sec-l18-temperature}

The thermodynamic identity for specific internal energy is

$$
de=T\,ds+\frac{P}{\rho^2}d\rho.
$$

Use continuity to obtain $\rho D_te=\rho TD_ts-P\nabla\cdot\mathbf v$. Comparing with @eq-l18-internal cancels compression work and gives

$$
\rho TD_ts=\tau_{ij}\partial_jv_i+
\nabla\cdot(\kappa\nabla T).
$$ {#eq-l18-entropy}

This is the material entropy equation, not yet the entropy production equation: conduction can raise or lower the entropy of a particular parcel by exchanging heat with its neighbors. Dividing by $T$ and moving a divergence to the left produces the nonnegative local production $\kappa|\nabla T|^2/T^2+\tau_{ij}\partial_jv_i/T$ for positive transport coefficients.

If pressure variations have a negligible thermal effect, $ds\simeq(c_p/T)dT$, where $c_p$ is specific heat at constant pressure. Assuming constant coefficients,

$$
\rho c_pD_tT=\kappa\nabla^2T+\tau_{ij}\partial_jv_i.
$$ {#eq-l18-temperature-heating}

The approximation matters for gases: the more general temperature equation contains a pressure work term, $\rho c_pD_tT-\beta T D_tP=\kappa\nabla^2T+\tau_{ij}\partial_jv_i$, where $\beta$ is the volume expansion coefficient. The simplified equation is appropriate when that term can be neglected.

Compare viscous heating $\eta U^2/L^2$ with conduction $\kappa\Delta T/L^2$. Their ratio is the Brinkman number,

$$
\mathrm{Br}=\frac{\eta U^2}{\kappa\Delta T}.
$$ {#eq-l18-brinkman}

For $\mathrm{Br}\ll1$, discard viscous heating and define thermal diffusivity $\chi=\kappa/(\rho c_p)$:

$$
\partial_tT+\mathbf v\cdot\nabla T=\chi\nabla^2T.
$$ {#eq-l18-advection-diffusion}

Convection is heat carried by moving fluid. Conduction remains essential wherever temperature gradients create the heat flux into or out of that moving fluid.

## Forced convection at a heated plate {#sec-l18-forced}

Take a flat plate at $T_0+\Delta T$ in an incident flow at $T_0$. The viscous boundary layer has thickness $\delta_v\sim\sqrt{\nu x/U}$. Let $\delta_T$ be the thermal layer thickness. Their relation depends on the Prandtl number,

$$
\mathrm{Pr}=\frac{\nu}{\chi}.
$$ {#eq-l18-prandtl}

It compares momentum diffusion with thermal diffusion. Unlike Reynolds number, it depends only on material properties at a specified state.

For $\mathrm{Pr}\ll1$, heat diffuses much farther than momentum, so $\delta_T\gg\delta_v$. Most of the thermal layer sees approximately uniform speed $U$. Balance $U\Delta T/x$ with $\chi\Delta T/\delta_T^2$:

$$
\delta_T\sim\sqrt{\frac{\chi x}{U}}
=\delta_v\mathrm{Pr}^{-1/2}.
$$ {#eq-l18-low-pr}

The local wall heat flux magnitude is $q_w\sim\kappa\Delta T/\delta_T$, hence $q_w\sim\kappa\Delta T\sqrt{U/(\chi x)}$. A faster flow thins the thermal layer and increases heat transfer.

For $\mathrm{Pr}\gg1$, the thermal layer lies within the nearly linear near wall velocity profile: $u\sim U y/\delta_v$. At its edge, the relevant speed is only $U\delta_T/\delta_v$. The balance becomes

$$
\frac{U\delta_T}{\delta_v}\frac{\Delta T}{x}
\sim\frac{\chi\Delta T}{\delta_T^2},
\qquad
\delta_T\sim\left(\frac{\chi x\delta_v}{U}\right)^{1/3}
=\delta_v\mathrm{Pr}^{-1/3}.
$$ {#eq-l18-high-pr}

Accordingly $q_w\sim\kappa\Delta T\,\mathrm{Pr}^{1/3}/\delta_v$. The cube root arises because the advecting speed itself depends on the unknown thermal thickness. Using $U$ throughout this thin thermal layer would give the wrong exponent. These are scaling estimates for a laminar layer; numerical prefactors require a coupled similarity calculation and specified thermal boundary conditions.

## When temperature drives the flow {#sec-l18-boussinesq}

Forced convection prescribes the flow independently of heating. Natural convection instead arises because thermal expansion changes gravitational buoyancy. Define

$$
\beta=-\frac1\rho\left(\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial T}\right)_P>0,
\qquad
\rho(T)\simeq\rho_0[1-\beta(T-T_0)].
$$ {#eq-l18-expansion}

Assume $\beta\Delta T\ll1$, so density changes are small. The Boussinesq approximation keeps this change in the gravitational force, where it drives motion, and replaces density by $\rho_0$ in inertia, viscosity, and continuity. With upward vertical direction $\hat{\mathbf y}$ and hydrostatic background pressure subtracted,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\nabla\cdot\mathbf v&=0,\\
D_t\mathbf v&=-\frac{\nabla\pi}{\rho_0}+\nu\nabla^2\mathbf v
+g\beta(T-T_0)\hat{\mathbf y},\\
D_tT&=\chi\nabla^2T.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-l18-boussinesq}

Hotter fluid experiences upward buoyancy. There is no contradiction between this retained density correction and leading incompressibility: it is a controlled approximation in which the dominant uniform gravitational force has already been canceled by hydrostatic pressure.

The assumption that density changes arise mainly from temperature also constrains pressure induced compression. With $(\partial\rho/\partial P)\sim1/c_s^2$, require $\Delta P/(\rho_0c_s^2)\ll\beta\Delta T$ when neglecting that contribution relative to thermal expansion. Across a height $L$, hydrostatic compression is of order $gL/c_s^2$. Thin laboratory cells often satisfy the required hierarchy; tall atmospheric columns require a stratified description.

## A side heated box: solving the weak flow limit {#sec-l18-box}

Consider a square cavity of side $L$, hot at $x=0$ and cold at $x=L$. Assume weak advection, insulating top and bottom, and stationary walls. To leading order conduction gives

$$
T=T_0+\Delta T\left(1-\frac{x}{L}\right).
$$

Also suppose inertia is negligible. Set $v_x=\partial_y\psi$ and $v_y=-\partial_x\psi$. Taking the curl of the Stokes–buoyancy equation removes pressure:

$$
\nabla^4\psi=-\frac{g\beta\Delta T}{\nu L}.
$$ {#eq-l18-biharmonic}

The sign follows our upward $y$ convention. Hot fluid rises along the left wall and cold fluid descends at the right. A particular solution is

$$
\psi_p=-\frac{g\beta\Delta T}{64\nu L}(x^2+y^2)^2,
$$

because $\nabla^4(x^2+y^2)^2=64$. This polynomial alone does not satisfy the walls. Add a homogeneous biharmonic solution and enforce $\psi=\partial_n\psi=0$ on every wall, representing no penetration and no slip. The detailed boundary value solution is less illuminating than its characteristic balance,

$$
\nu\frac{U_{\mathrm{visc}}}{L^2}\sim g\beta\Delta T,
\qquad U_{\mathrm{visc}}\sim\frac{g\beta\Delta T L^2}{\nu}.
$$ {#eq-l18-viscous-speed}

The conductive temperature profile additionally needs small Péclet number $\mathrm{Pe}=UL/\chi$. A small Reynolds number alone does not guarantee weak thermal advection.

## Checking the estimate and restoring inertia {#sec-l18-inertial}

For an ideal gas, $\beta=1/T$. Even a modest $\beta\Delta T\sim0.01$ in air with $\nu\sim10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m^2\,s^{-1}}$ gives $U_{\mathrm{visc}}\sim10^4\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ at $L=1\ \mathrm m$. This absurdly large prediction rejects the weak flow assumption, rather than predicting a supersonic kitchen oven.

When inertia balances buoyancy, use $U^2/L\sim g\beta\Delta T$ instead:

$$
U_{\mathrm{ff}}\sim\sqrt{g\beta\Delta T L}.
$$ {#eq-l18-freefall}

At $L=1\ \mathrm m$ and $\beta\Delta T=0.01$, this is roughly $0.3\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. It is a characteristic free fall estimate; walls, heat supply, and thermal boundary layers determine the actual circulation.

A useful supplemental parameter is the Grashof number $\mathrm{Gr}=g\beta\Delta TL^3/\nu^2$. The viscous estimate implies $\mathrm{Re}\sim\mathrm{Gr}$, so it requires $\mathrm{Gr}\ll1$. The Rayleigh number $\mathrm{Ra}=\mathrm{Gr}\,\mathrm{Pr}$ also compares buoyancy with thermal diffusion. This side heated cavity should not be confused with a bottom heated Rayleigh–Bénard layer: its lateral buoyancy forcing can drive circulation without the same onset threshold.

## Common pitfalls

Thermal conductivity $\kappa$ and diffusivity $\chi$ have different units. High Prandtl number means heat diffuses slowly relative to momentum. Incompressibility does not require deleting buoyancy. A velocity estimate must be checked against the inertial and thermal terms that were neglected in obtaining it.

## Exercises with solutions {#sec-l18-exercises}

1. **Thermal thickness.** If $\mathrm{Pr}=1000$, estimate $\delta_T/\delta_v$ in the high Prandtl regime.

   **Solution.** @eq-l18-high-pr gives $1000^{-1/3}=0.1$. The thermal layer samples velocities much smaller than the exterior speed.

2. **Cavity size.** At fixed material parameters and temperature difference, how do viscous and free fall speeds change if $L$ doubles?

   **Solution.** $U_{\mathrm{visc}}$ increases by four, whereas $U_{\mathrm{ff}}$ increases by $\sqrt2$. The rapidly increasing Grashof number, proportional to $L^3$, explains why a creeping estimate breaks down in larger cells.

3. **Dimensions and heat flux.** Why is $\kappa\Delta T/\delta_T$ a heat flux rather than a temperature change rate?

   **Solution.** $[\kappa]=\mathrm{W\,m^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$, so the expression has units $\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$. Dividing the divergence of heat flux by volumetric heat capacity $\rho c_p$ yields a temperature change rate, as in @eq-l18-advection-diffusion.
